core_principles.text: Start in a high plank with hands slightly wider than shoulder width, fingers spread, abs braced, and glutes squeezed to form a straight line from head to heel.
Lower under control until the chest reaches a consistent depth close to the floor.
Press back to straight arms without allowing the hips to sag, rise first, or twist.
Keep the neck neutral by looking a short distance ahead of the hands.
Maintain a moderate elbow angle relative to the torso rather than aggressively flaring them.

common_mistakes.text: Performing partial repetitions where the chest does not lower close to the floor.
Allowing the hips to sag toward the floor or rise before the upper body.
Continuing repetitions after resting in a broken plank position.
Bouncing repetitions off the bottom position.

specific_findings.text: In a large prospective study of active adult men, greater baseline push-up capacity was associated with lower subsequent cardiovascular event risk.
Research comparing push-up and bench press training found similar gains in muscle thickness and strength when the exercises were performed with comparable effort and suitable loading.

consequences.text: Failing to brace the abdominals and glutes during push-ups allows the lower back to extend into excessive arching.

core_principles.text: Maintain consistent depth and body position across all repetitions without allowing form to break down.
Use push-up handles or securely placed dumbbells to adopt a neutral wrist position if wrist discomfort occurs.
If experiencing front shoulder pain, temporarily reduce range of motion, use an incline, check elbow path, or reduce pressing volume.
Pair pressing exercises with pulling movements like rows and chin-ups to ensure good scapular motion.

common_mistakes.text: Starting a timed push-up set too quickly rather than pacing conservatively.
Allowing depth or body position to break down under fatigue during high-repetition tests.

consequences.text: Starting a timed push-up test too fast causes the chest and triceps to fatigue faster than they can recover, making later repetitions dramatically harder.
